news.headline: Dipke gets exemption from in-person appearance before magistrate on medical grounds
news.story_lead: Dipke gets exemption from in-person appearance before magistrate on medical grounds The SEM at Mandir Marg police station allowed the exemption on Tuesday after Abhijeet Dipke’s counsel cited medical grounds for his absence. Cockroach Janta Party ( CJP ) founder Abhijeet Dipke has been granted an exemption from appearing in-person before the special executive magistrate (SEM) regarding the preventive inquiry against him. The SEM at Mandir Marg police station allowed the exemption on Tuesday after Dipke’s counsel, Abhik Chimni, cited medical grounds for his absence.
news.full_article_text: Dipke gets exemption from in-person appearance before magistrate on medical grounds The SEM at Mandir Marg police station allowed the exemption on Tuesday after Abhijeet Dipke’s counsel cited medical grounds for his absence. Cockroach Janta Party ( CJP ) founder Abhijeet Dipke has been granted an exemption from appearing in-person before the special executive magistrate (SEM) regarding the preventive inquiry against him. The SEM at Mandir Marg police station allowed the exemption on Tuesday after Dipke’s counsel, Abhik Chimni, cited medical grounds for his absence. The matter has been posted for December 2 for further proceedings. During the proceedings, Chimni was also provided copies of the “kalandra” (preventive police report) and other legal documents that the Delhi Police relied on to issue Dipke a show-cause notice, asking him to furnish a bond for maintaining peace. ALSO READ: CJP’s Abhijeet Dipke says he spent night at airport on way back from Kochi protest This development comes weeks after Dipke was granted conditional bail by an SEM following his arrest over an alleged breach of a peace bond he furnished earlier. One principal condition imposed on him was that he must ensure no breach of peace on his part for a period of one year. Dipke was detained on October 16 while heading towards Connaught Place for a protest march called by the CJP under the banner of ‘Lehra Do Tiranga’. The march was called despite a Delhi Police notice asking him not to participate, citing prohibitory orders under Section 163 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita (BNSS). ALSO READ: CJP’s Abhijeet Dipke predicts ‘Modi govt’s defeat in 2029’ at anti-SIR rally in Kochi: ‘He will definitely go’ He was subsequently arrested on October 17 for allegedly violating a peace bond furnished on October 10. He was later released on a conditional bail bond by the special executive magistrate. The bond was intended to secure an undertaking from him to maintain peace and prevent any disturbance to public order for a year. - ABOUT THE AUTHOR Arnabjit Sur Arnabjit Sur is a Senior Correspondent with Hindustan Times who primarily covers stories from the capital's trial courts. news.headline: Meet the Peaky Blinders, Ukraine's drone unit protecting a devastated front-line city
news.story_lead: Meet the Peaky Blinders, Ukraine's drone unit protecting a devastated front-line city The BBC's Jonathan Beale reported from inside Slovyansk, one of four cities that make up Ukraine's "fortress belt" - a system of heavily reinforced defence lines in the parts of eastern region of Donetsk still under its control. The town has become almost uninhabitable and has been under heavy bombardment from Russian drones, missiles and glide bombs. Members of a Ukrainian drone unit that call themselves Peaky Blinders, named after the cult BBC TV series, have taken on the task of intercepting Russian drones.

Najib's return ended a four-year prison stint after he was found guilty over the embezzlement of billions of dollars from the country's sovereign wealth fund. Investigators estimated that $4.5bn (Â£3.3bn) was siphoned from the state-owned wealth fund, which Najib co-founded, into private pockets, including his own. More than $1bn allegedly ended up in accounts linked to Najib, according to prosecutors. Najib's lawyers claim he had been misled by his advisers - in particular the financier Jho Low, who has maintained his innocence and remains at large. Journalists jostled for a glimpse of Najib as he was driven to his home, which has been declared a federal prison Najib's mansion in one of the capital's most exclusive neighbourhoods was declared a federal prison ahead of his homecoming on Tuesday. Critics said his release from jail undermined efforts to fight corruption and questioned its legal basis, saying Malaysian law made no provision for house arrest. Najib, who was prime minister from 2009 to 2018, denied wrongdoing but was convicted at two separate trials. In the first trial he was sentenced in 2020 to 12 years in prison and jailed in 2022. The term was later halved on appeal. In September, the King of Malaysia granted him a conditional pardon to see out the remaining two years of his sentence at home. The transfer to his mansion was to take place on Friday but put on hold after the attorney general sought clarification of the royal decree. On Tuesday the high court ruled the house arrest was effective immediately. Najib's party paid a $12m fine as part of the terms of the royal pardon allowing him to serve the rest of his term at home. He was sentenced after being convicted of abuse of power, money laundering and breach of trust over 42 million ringgit ($10m; Â£7.7m) transferred from SRC International - a former unit of 1MDB - into his private accounts. Najib is appealing against a 15-year prison sentence, handed down at a second trial in December 2025 , in a case involving much larger sums of money. In that case he was convicted of misappropriating nearly 2.3 billion Malaysian ringgit ($569m; Â£422m) from the nation's sovereign wealth fund 1Malaysia Development Berhad (1MDB). news.full_article_text: As Delhi gasps for clean air, pollution in NCR dropped from Parliament panel meeting agenda The Parliamentary Committee on Home Affairs had earlier decided to hear the views of the Ministry of Home Affairs and agencies concerned and discuss the issue. As Delhi struggles with polluted air, a Parliamentary committee has decided to drop the key issue of air pollution in NCR from the agenda of its November 17 meeting, prompting a Congress member to raise strong objections with the panel chairperson. The Parliamentary Committee on Home Affairs had earlier decided to hear the views of the Ministry of Home Affairs and agencies concerned on the issue and hold a discussion. The panel circulated the agenda for the meeting, which included the air pollution issue, among its members on November 5, but dropped the topic from its revised agenda. Also Read | AQI of 387 in India would be nearly 1,500 in US and 10 in UK. Why the range is so wide Congress member Ajay Maken has raised strong objections to the omission of the air pollution issue and has written to the committee chairperson, Radha Mohan Das Agrawal. Agrawal, when contacted, said he was not aware of the letter by Ajay Maken. "I am ignorant of the letter," he told PTI when asked about Maken's letter to him. On why the pollution issue was dropped in the revised agenda, Agrawal said he does not discuss issues relating to the Committee meetings in public. The earlier agenda for the panel meeting stated, "To hear the views of Ministry of Home Affairs and concerned agencies on the subject 'Air pollution in Delhi-NCR: Enforcement of Regulatory measures, effective implementation of GRAP measures, protection of vulnerable sections and coordination among law enforcement and government agencies." The amended agenda has omitted the air pollution issue and will now only hear the views of the Ministry of Ports, Shipping and Waterways as well as the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment on the issue of "drug trafficking and narcotics control: Emerging threats and institutional response". "I wish to register my objection to the omission of the air-pollution hearing from the revised agenda for 17 November 2026. Given the urgency of the health risks, I request that this change be reconsidered and the hearing restored to that date," Maken said in his letter to Agrawal. "I therefore request restoration of the air-pollution hearing on 17 November. If restoration is not possible, please fix and communicate the earliest firm alternative date, together with the reason for the change. I would be grateful for a response before the scheduled meeting," the Congress MP said. Maken said he had requested examination of air pollution in his letter of November 2 and thanked the committee chairperson for including the subject in its programme for 2026-27, as published in Bulletin Part II dated November 6, No. 66837 as item 13. "The original public notice dated 5 November scheduled the hearing with the Ministry of Home Affairs and concerned agencies for 17 November at 2 p.m. The revised public notice dated 6 November omits that hearing. It gives no reason for this change," he said in his letter to the panel chairperson. Maken demanded that the Parliamentary Standing Committee on Home Affairs restore its hearing on air pollution. "The official meeting schedule, read at 12:56 IST on 10 November, lists sittings on 16 and 17 November with no air-pollution item on either day, and no new date has been notified," he said. Also Read | High pollution alert issued in London after PM2.5 levels exceed WHO limits by 8 times Maken said Delhi's air-pollution crisis must be treated as a public-health emergency. "A reading of 500 is a ceiling and not the actual reading, because CPCB's index is capped at 500. CPCB's own calculator has severe-band formulas that run on above 500, but a display cap reduces every result above 500 to 500. news.full_article_text: Gadi Eisenkot has vowed to oust Benjamin Netanyahu, but still has to get enough parties on board - Published 10 November 2026, 12:25 GMT Israel's new parliament has been sworn in, as opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot seeks to oust caretaker Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The former army chief has been tasked with forming a government after receiving more recommendations from members of the Knesset than Netanyahu, although not all those backing him are willing to govern together. Eisenkot's bloc of four parties won 48 seats in October's election, while Netanyahu's bloc won 53, leaving both short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. He has 28 days to build a coalition, with a possible two-week extension. Almost half of the new MKs did not serve in the previous parliament, while Arab-led parties have a record number of seats. Shortly after they were sworn in, Netanyahu and Eisenkot warned parliament about the perils of supporting a government led by the other. "[And] to those who are thinking of establishing a government that includes supporters of terror and haters of Israel, or that will be dependent on them, I ask you, are you prepared to be dependent on those whose goal is the destruction of the Jewish state?" said Netanyahu, alluding to the prospect of an Eisenkot-led government reliant on support from Arab parties. He also appealed for the formation of a government of national unity as the only way to confront what he said was the threat of "a nuclear Iran". Eisenkot sharply criticised Netanyahu's comments. "I sat and listened to the outgoing prime minister's delusional, divisive, hate-filled and shameful speech, exploiting a state occasion," he said. "I am now even more convinced that he is unfit to remain in office for even one more minute." The outcome of the election, which was widely seen as a referendum on Netanyahu, means there is a period of uncertainty over who will form the next government. Netanyahu will remain caretaker prime minister until then - a process which could take from days to months. One of the most dramatic results was the performance of Israel's two Arab-led alliances - the United Arab List and the Joint List - which won an unprecedented 19 seats between them following a surge in turnout among Arab voters. The Arab parties could therefore hold the balance of power, although Netanyahu has ruled out governing with them and three of the parties in Eisenkot's bloc have opposed including them in a coalition. On Sunday, President Isaac Herzog tasked Eisenkot with trying to form a government. Speaking at the president's residence, the centrist Yashar party leader called for the formation of a "national emergency government" - an implicit appeal to parties to put ideological differences aside to remove Netanyahu from office. This, he said, would "require creative and unconventional political steps". Eisenkot said any party or MK prepared to accept four principles could join his proposed government. Those are recognition of Israel as a Jewish and democratic state; accepting the values of the Declaration of Independence; backing mandatory military, national or civilian service for all, including communities currently exempt; and recognising Hamas as a terrorist organisation and committing to dismantling its military and governing capabilities. The four requirements, however, could present significant obstacles to Eisenkot's potential partners. The conscription of ultra-Orthodox Jewish men, who are exempt from military service if they are in full-time religious study, was a major election issue. The ultra-Orthodox United Torah Judaism (UTJ) and Shas parties, which won 13 seats in total, have fiercely objected to attempts to change the status quo - something that all parties in Eisenkot's bloc campaigned to do. Eisenkot's four principles are also contentious for the Arab parties. Both emphasise equal national and civic rights for Israel's Arab citizens, who form about 20% of the population; the vast majority of Israeli Arabs are not required to serve in the military; and neither has publicly recognised Hamas as a terrorist organisation. The Arab parties could, though, help Eisenkot form a minority government. The United Arab List, which won eight seats, has said it is willing to be part of an Eisenkot-led coalition, while the Joint List, which won 11 seats, has offered parliamentary support from the outside. If Eisenkot accepted such an arrangement, he would still have to persuade other parties in his bloc to agree. Avigdor Lieberman, whose Yisrael Beiteinu party won seven seats, has so far refused to join a minority government dependent on Arab MKs. In return for their support, the ultra-Orthodox parties would be likely to demand major concessions on military conscription, which might be unacceptable to most of the parties in Eisenkot's bloc.
